reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: Benign oedematous outgrowths of inflamed sinonasal mucosa presenting with nasal obstruction, reduced smell and rhinorrhoea
Bilateral multiple ethmoidal polyps are typically associated with chronic rhinosinusitis, allergy and asthma
A single antrochoanal polyp usually arises from the maxillary sinus, is more common in younger patients, and extends toward the posterior nasal space
Polyps appear as pale, smooth, mobile, insensitive glistening masses on anterior rhinoscopy or endoscopy
The association of nasal polyps, asthma and aspirin sensitivity is a recognised clinical triad
Management principles combine intranasal and, where needed, short courses of systemic corticosteroids with treatment of underlying allergy and infection
Endoscopic sinus surgery is considered when medical therapy fails or obstruction is severe, though recurrence is common
Unilateral polyps, bleeding, or atypical appearance warrant biopsy and imaging to exclude malignancy or other lesions
reference.pathophysiology: Nasal polyps are pedunculated masses of oedematous, chronically inflamed sinonasal mucosa, most often stemming from persistent inflammation in the ethmoid region. Ongoing mucosal inflammation, frequently eosinophil-rich, causes fluid accumulation within the lamina propria, and gravity together with impaired lymphatic drainage encourages the mucosa to prolapse into the nasal cavity as polyps. Contributing factors include chronic rhinosinusitis, allergy, aspirin sensitivity and, in children, cystic fibrosis. The antrochoanal polyp arises from maxillary sinus mucosa, passes through its ostium and enlarges into the choana and nasopharynx.
additionalDifferentials: Hypertrophied inferior turbinate mistaken for a polyp
additionalInvestigations: Nasal endoscopy to characterise and localise the polyps
CT of the paranasal sinuses to define extent and plan surgery
Allergy testing where an allergic component is suspected
Histopathology of excised or atypical tissue to exclude neoplasm
Investigation for cystic fibrosis in children with polyps
redFlags: Unilateral polyp with bleeding or an atypical firm appearance suggesting malignancy or angiofibroma
Orbital signs such as proptosis, diplopia or visual disturbance indicating spread
A polypoidal mass in a child that could be an encephalocoele, warranting caution before biopsy
Rapid growth, facial pain or cranial nerve involvement
reference.prognosis: Nasal polyps are benign but tend to be chronic and recurrent, particularly in association with asthma and aspirin sensitivity; symptoms are usually controllable with combined medical and surgical management, though repeated treatment is often needed.
pitfalls: Assuming all nasal masses are benign polyps and missing a tumour or angiofibroma
Biopsying a suspected polyp in a child without first excluding an encephalocoele
Relying on surgery alone without ongoing medical control of underlying inflammation
Overlooking associated asthma and aspirin sensitivity
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: First-line intranasal corticosteroids to shrink polyps and suppress mucosal inflammation
Short courses of systemic corticosteroids for severe obstruction or failure of topical therapy
Regular saline nasal irrigation alongside treatment of coexisting allergic rhinitis with antihistamines or leukotriene receptor antagonists
Endoscopic sinus surgery (polypectomy or functional endoscopic sinus surgery) for polyps refractory to medical therapy or for an obstructing antrochoanal polyp
Biologic therapy targeting type 2 inflammation, such as anti-IL-4Ralpha or anti-IL-5 agents, for severe recurrent eosinophilic disease
In aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, avoid NSAIDs and consider aspirin desensitisation
Screen children with polyps for cystic fibrosis
Long-term ENT follow-up with endoscopic surveillance for recurrence
